title: When is a talent decision implemented? A two-condition test for HR leaders
abstract: Purpose Talent decisions are usually marked complete when the administrative transaction closes. This paper aims to ask a different question: Has the organisation put the associated work change into operation? Design/methodology/approach The paper brings together selected work on talent management, work design and role transitions. A published Australian Transport Safety Bureau investigation and a fictional service-business scenario are used to show where administrative closure and operational implementation can diverge. Findings A talent transaction can close on time even though important former responsibilities remain unsettled or the new arrangement is not yet working as intended. The paper proposes a separate operational status, confirmed when each relevant prior work arrangement has been dealt with and the new arrangement is operating with the agreed initial scope, authority and availability. The first condition is not applicable to many genuinely new roles. Practical implications HR can use the test in existing business or talent reviews without holding open contracts, effective dates or other completed transactions. Originality/value The paper treats implementation as an organisational work question, rather than assuming that a completed people transaction means the underlying decision has taken effect.

title: When emotions matter: the contextual effectiveness of emotional expressions in AI agents
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) agents’ emotional expressions (positive or neutral) interact with service task types (subjective or objective) to shape consumer service satisfaction, and explore the mediating roles of mind perception, including perceived agency and perceived experience, in this process. Design/methodology/approach This work uses four studies, including a secondary data analysis of relevant Weibo posts and three scenario experiments involving a total of 587 participants, to underline the interaction effect between AI agents’ emotional expressions and service tasks on service satisfaction, and demonstrate the dual-path mediating effect of mind perception. Findings Across four studies, the authors find that the effectiveness of AI agents’ emotional expressions depends on service task characteristics. The secondary data analysis of Weibo posts first documents consumers’ differential responses to AI emotional expressions across subjective and objective service contexts. Three scenario experiments then establish that positive emotional expressions are more effective for subjective tasks, whereas neutral emotional expressions are more effective for objective tasks. Further analyses show that these effects operate through distinct psychological pathways: positive emotions enhance perceived experience in subjective tasks, whereas neutral emotions strengthen perceived agency in objective tasks, ultimately increasing consumer satisfaction. Research limitations/implications This study, while strong in internal validity, faces external validity limitations. It focuses on AI communication in commercial service texts, neglecting other domains like education and health care, and overlooking the nonverbal emotional expressions of embodied AI. In addition, the research primarily uses service satisfaction as the sole dependent variable, thus missing a broader spectrum of consumer responses such as repurchase intentions and word-of-mouth. Practical implications This research informs managers that AI service agents should be designed as social actors with mind perception rather than as purely functional tools. Firms can leverage emotional expressions to shape consumers’ social evaluations of AI. But emotional design should align with service task types: positive emotional cues are more effective for subjective, experiential tasks, whereas neutral styles better support objective, data-driven tasks. Originality/value This study contributes to the emotional AI literature by uncovering critical situational factors that shape the effectiveness of AI emotional expressions and advances the authors’ understanding of the underlying mechanisms through a dual-path mediation framework of mind perception. The findings also provide practical implications for the strategic deployment of emotional AI in service design.

title: The perception of craft construction workers on the application of artificial intelligence in health and safety in UK construction
journal: Journal of Engineering, Design and Technology
abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is starting to play a bigger role in health and safety (H&S) in UK construction. While most studies today are concerned about managerial perceptions, technological possibilities and organisational readiness, there is a dearth of research on the use of AI based on the lived experiences of construction workers. This research aims to explore how craft construction workers perceive the application of AI in construction H&S. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was used to garner the data to achieve the research aim. Overall, 20 craft construction workers with 5–20 years of experience were purposively selected from the UK (England, Scotland and Wales) and interviewed. The data were analysed using thematic analysis. Findings The findings revealed a slow but gradual uptake of AI-enabled H&S tools, and AI is mostly used for hazard warning on construction sites. Some workers view AI as a beneficial modern addition; others perceive it as a form of surveillance. In addition, workers’ age influenced their attitudes towards AI, and the clarity of AI tools’ functions influenced how workers accepted them. One benefit of AI is hazard detection, but workers lack trust in its reliability. Practical implications The findings reported in this study will assist the construction industry, policymakers and technology developers in addressing concerns about AI in H&S while leveraging the benefits associated with their usage. Originality/value This study is among the first qualitative studies to empirically explore the perspective of key stakeholders (frontline workers−craft construction workers) in the UK on the application of AI in construction H&S management. This study contributes to future AI adoption in construction H&S management in the UK.

title: The illusion of algorithmic belonging: why generative AI cannot substitute for relational reciprocity in mental health social inclusion
abstract: Purpose This study aims to critically discuss the fast-moving rollout of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and conversational agents as purported remedies to loneliness and social isolation, analysing the fact that the creation of companionship by algorithms substitutes a one-way connection and fundamentally jeopardises real social inclusion. Design/methodology/approach An interdisciplinary perspective that draws from relational sociology, the social model of disability, critical digital studies and various literatures on psychiatric rehabilitation to critique the inter-personal ethics, psychological dangers and political economy of digital mental health companions. It also comprises a comparative analysis of the existing market leaders in conversational AI. Findings Proximate affective containment is provided by generative AI, but lacks of relational reciprocity, moral agency and shared vulnerability. The replacement of civic infrastructures in community settings by automated, conversational agents can set up a divided mental health system: human-centred relational mental health care for the privileged and synthetic, automated containment for the marginalised service user. Moreover, AI companionship takes out user vulnerability as property information, turns it into a commodity, the lived experience of solitude. Research limitations/implications As a perspective, this paper does not contain empirical data of its own; it constructs the argument by conceptual synthesis instead of a systematic review, and the examples of markets discussed (e.g. Woebot, Wysa, Replika) are illustrative, but not comprehensive or evaluative of current versions of products and so may have changed significantly since the time of writing. Longitudinal studies that compare the outcomes of service users using algorithmic companionship with peer-support and Clubhouse models will confirm the synthetic inclusion construct developed here, and could be used for future research. Practical implications Offers evaluative tools to the mental health commissioners, clinicians and third sector organisations to avoid the “community replacement” trap of digital engagement, keeping AI a cognitive prosthetic and not a substitute for interpersonal interactions. Social implications Disciplines policymakers from adopting techno-solutionism as an excuse for austerity-driven disinvestment of physical community centres, peer respites and inclusive civic spaces and calls for the protection of the human social commons. Originality/value This paper outlines the concept of a “synthetic inclusion” that reveals that the illusion of connection created by conversational AI is a commodity, and that social isolation is structurally reinforced. It contributes to the critique of mental health in the digital age by examining unconstrained large language models from a perspective of surveillance capitalism and intersectionality.

title: The adaptive coordination and administrative resilience: lessons from European Union (EU) migration governance
abstract: Purpose This article examines how repeated coordination practices contribute to administrative resilience in multilevel systems undergoing formal institutional change. Focusing on European Union (EU) migration governance, it asks how coordinated action continues when responsibility remains divided and crisis pressure recurs. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a qualitative, longitudinal single-case design covering 2015-2024. Ten Commission, agency, audit, and legislative documents are analysed chronologically by actors, timing, task allocation, and procedural formalisation. The design traces operational change rather than measuring policy performance or testing causal effects. Findings Formal reforms expanded mandates, resources, and coordination structures but did not determine daily cooperation. The analysis identifies four overlapping stages: disruption, improvisation, stabilisation, and preparedness. Disruption exposed registration gaps and unclear roles. Improvisation made the centrally designed hotspot framework workable through practical clarification of responsibilities and procedures. Stabilisation followed as agencies organised support, deployment planning, and information exchange through recurring plans and structures. Preparedness emerged as monitoring, early warning, and advance planning began before full crisis activation. Resilience therefore rested on interaction between institutional capacity and repeated operational cooperation, not on either formal redesign or informal practice alone. The evidence indicates an emerging but uneven capacity for earlier coordination, rather than a completed or uniformly effective system. Originality/value The article develops an adaptive coordination cycle centred on implementation rather than policy design. It distinguishes operational resilience from policy success and explains how repeated interaction can make coordination more predictable before it is fully formalised. The framework applies conditionally to multilevel systems with shared competence and limited hierarchical control.

title: The Challenges Associated with the Diagnosis and Treatment for Aplastic Anemia Concurrent with Lymphoplasmacytic Lymphoma/Waldenström's Macroglobulinemia
Peran Motivasi dalam Memediasi Pengaruh Soft Skill terhadap Kesiapan Kerja Mahasiswa
journal: Global Leadership Organizational Research in Management
abstract: The increasingly competitive nature of the labor market requires university students not only to possess strong academic competencies but also to develop work readiness supported by soft skills and motivation. This study aims to examine the effect of soft skills on students’ work readiness, with motivation serving as an intervening variable among students of the Faculty of Economics and Business at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional “Veteran” Jawa Timur. This research employed a quantitative approach using primary data collected through an online questionnaire. The population of this study consisted of active students from the 2021 cohort of the Faculty of Economics and Business at UPN “Veteran” Jawa Timur, with a sample of 150 respondents. The data were analyzed using the Partial Least Squares (PLS) method with the assistance of SmartPLS software. The results indicate that soft skills have a positive and significant effect on motivation. Furthermore, motivation has a positive and significant effect on work readiness. Soft skills also have a direct, positive, and significant effect on work readiness. The analysis of the indirect effect further demonstrates that motivation significantly mediates the relationship between soft skills and work readiness. Based on these findings, it can be concluded that the development of soft skills and motivation are interconnected in supporting students’ readiness to face the demands of and enter the workforce. The study implies that higher education institutions can strengthen students’ preparation for employment by integrating activities that develop communication, critical thinking, collaboration, self-management, and career-oriented motivation.
